title: Plate with David Anointed by Samuel

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A round silver plate with a scene in raised figures. A man pours oil on the head of a young man, David, as other figures look on.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, culture (Byzantine), classification (Metalwork-Silver), tags (Rams, David), dimensions, credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A silver plate made in the Byzantine Empire in 629–630. It belongs to the group known as the David Plates, found on Cyprus, which show episodes from the life of David as told in the Bible. This one shows the prophet Samuel anointing David.

descriptions.k: This is a shiny silver plate. A man named Samuel pours oil on David's head. In the story, this means David will become a king. The plate was made more than 1,300 years ago. Who do you see in the picture?
descriptions.g12: Long ago, a metalworker made this silver plate in the Byzantine Empire. It shows a story from the Bible. The prophet Samuel pours oil on David to show he will one day be a king. David watched over sheep, so look for an animal in the picture. How do you think David feels?
descriptions.g35: This silver plate was made in the Byzantine Empire in 629–630. It is one of a set of nine found on Cyprus, and each plate shows a scene from the life of David, a shepherd who becomes a king in the Bible. Here the prophet Samuel anoints David by pouring oil on his head. The plate is about 26 centimeters wide and weighs more than a kilogram. Look at the figures' poses. How does the artist show who is important?
descriptions.g68: This is one of the David Plates, nine silver plates found on Cyprus and dated to 629–630, during the reign of Emperor Heraclius. Each shows an episode from David's life as told in the Bible. Here Samuel anoints David, marking him as a future king. The metalworker had to tell the story clearly inside a circle, using the arrangement, gestures, and clothing of the figures. Some scholars link the series to the emperor's own image as a ruler chosen by God, though this is debated. What visual choices make the central action easy to read?
descriptions.g910: The David Plates, made in 629–630 and found on Cyprus, combine biblical narrative with the visual language of Byzantine court art. Here Samuel anoints David, and the metalworker relies on figure arrangement and gesture to emphasize a sacred moment. The classical-looking figures show how Byzantine art continued older Roman models. Scholars debate whether the series carried a political message tied to Emperor Heraclius, since David was a model of a divinely chosen ruler. How do composition and the sheer weight and value of silver help convey importance?
descriptions.g1112: The David Plates are a rare survival of seventh-century Byzantine silverwork, linked by control stamps to the reign of Heraclius, around 629–630. This plate shows Samuel anointing David, a scene of divine selection that some scholars connect to imperial ideology after the emperor's campaigns against Persia; others caution that biblical narrative can be read without a political key. The classicizing figures suggest continuity with Roman art rather than a sharp break. How should we balance religious meaning, imperial context, and artistic tradition when reading a single object, and what evidence would be convincing for each?

k.daily: Samuel is pouring oil on David's head. What do you think David is feeling right then?

k.observation: Look for the people in the picture. How many can you find, and who looks most important?
k.analysis: Where do your eyes go first on this plate? What helps them go there?

k.texture: The people on the plate are raised up from the silver. How do you think they would feel to touch?
k.space: Which people are in front and which are behind? How can you tell?
k.light: Shiny silver bounces light back to your eyes. Where does the plate look brightest?
k.meaning: In the story, oil on the head means David will become a king. How do you think a person feels when they hear that?
k.culture: This plate was made in the Byzantine Empire, long ago. What special things in your home are made of metal?

g12.critical: How is a story told on a plate different from a story in a book? Which tells it better?

g35.emotion: What feeling does the scene have, ceremony, calm, or something else? Which details support your idea?

g1112.shape: How does the circular field create tension between centrality and the figures' individual outlines?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, culture, classification (Metalwork-Silver), medium and tags (Rams, David) checked against the Met Collection API record. The scene is a calm anointing; nothing in the metadata points to nudity, violence or frightening content. (The tags of other plates in the same set, such as the battle with Goliath, were not used.)

teacherNote.context: One of nine silver David Plates found on Cyprus and dated by control stamps to the reign of Heraclius, 629–630. Teach it as an example of Byzantine storytelling in precious metal, and note that scholars debate its political meaning.
directions: Ask students to retell the scene in a few sentences using only what they see, then compare with the story of David.
Have students sketch a circular design that tells a story with only three figures and one important gesture.
Discuss why leaders in different times have used images of chosen or special rulers.
